questions.why: Ce is the masculine singular form before a consonant. French has no separate word for this and that: ce livre is both.
Homme is masculine and its h is mute, so ce becomes cet to avoid two vowels colliding. Same for cet arbre and cet été.
Heure is feminine, and cette is used before anything, vowel or consonant. Cet would mean the noun was masculine.
Cet and cette sound identical, so only the noun's gender tells you which to write. Maison is feminine, so cette.

questions.q: Complete so it means « that book, over there »: « ce livre-___ »
questions.why: -ci marks the nearer thing, -là the further one, hyphenated onto the noun. In speech -là does most of the work as a general emphatic: ce mec-là.
Livre is masculine singular, so celui, and -là for the further one. Celle is feminine, ceux masculine plural.
Robe is feminine singular, and -ci marks the nearer one. The feminine plural would be celles-ci.

questions.q: Celui, celle, ceux and celles never stand alone. What must follow?
choices: -ci or -là, de, or a relative pronoun
questions.why: Celui-là, celui de mon frère, celui qui parle. On its own the pronoun is incomplete, which is why celui alone always sounds wrong.

questions.q: Complete: « ___ qui arrivent en retard attendront. » (Those who arrive late)
questions.why: Masculine plural celui becomes ceux, and here it is followed by the relative pronoun qui, which is one of the three legal continuations.

questions.q: Build the phrase: my opinion and my brother's
questions.why: Celui de replaces the repeated noun: literally the one of my brother. Celui is masculine because avis is.

questions.q: You are talking to a friend. Which sounds natural for « I like that » ?
questions.why: Ça is the spoken contraction of cela and dominates conversation; cela belongs to writing. Ce only ever appears before être.

questions.q: Complete: « ___ sont mes amis. » (These are my friends.)
questions.why: Ce is used only before être, and becomes ce sont before a plural noun. C'est mes amis is heard, but ce sont is the correct form.

questions.q: Which is correct for « He's a doctor », with no article?
questions.why: A bare profession takes il/elle est. Put an article in front and you must switch: c'est un médecin.
Cet links straight onto the mute h of homme, and -là points at him. Practising the join is the point here.

questions.q: When do you use « c'est » and when « il / elle est » ? Give two contrasting examples.
a: C'est before a noun with an article (c'est un professeur), before a name (c'est Marie), before a stressed pronoun (c'est moi) and for a general comment (c'est difficile). Il / elle est before a bare noun of profession (il est professeur) and before an adjective describing a known person (elle est difficile).
questions.why: The reliable trigger is what comes next: an article or a name pulls c'est, a bare profession or a personal adjective pulls il/elle est.
